image.subject: Ezekiel Cheever, a thin, officious court clerk in his forties in a dark brown coat, a black hat and a leather satchel of papers, Salem 1692, standing in the open doorway of a dark timber farmhouse kitchen at night holding out a folded paper warrant, while John Proctor, the bearded farmer in a leather vest, and Elizabeth Proctor, the Puritan wife in dark blue, face him by the candlelit hearth

storyboard.claim: Cheever arrives at the Proctor farmhouse with a warrant and asks about puppets.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Cheever in the doorway holding out the warrant to the Proctors at their hearth: the law physically entering the home.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the sequence at the Proctor hearth (kept stage for 118-120); the exchange rate from 117 now reaches a named household.
storyboard.addedInformation: The court's arrest power has arrived at Proctor's own door.

image.subject: Ezekiel Cheever, a thin, officious court clerk in his forties in a dark brown coat, a black hat and a leather satchel of papers, Salem 1692, reaching up to a stone fireplace mantle in a dim candlelit farmhouse kitchen to take down a small handmade cloth rag doll, while Elizabeth Proctor, the Puritan wife in dark blue, watches from behind him

storyboard.claim: Elizabeth denies keeping puppets, but Cheever finds the doll Mary Warren gave her.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Cheever's hand lifting the cloth doll off the mantle while Elizabeth watches: the denial contradicted by an object.
storyboard.onScreenText: THE POPPET · A GIFT FROM MARY WARREN
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same hearth, one step on: the question becomes a found object.
storyboard.addedInformation: The doll was a gift from the servant Mary Warren, given hours earlier.

image.subject: close photograph of the thin hands of a court clerk in a dark brown coat sleeve drawing a long steel sewing needle out of the belly of a small handmade cloth rag doll, candlelight in a dark farmhouse kitchen, Salem 1692

storyboard.claim: Cheever pulls a needle from the doll's belly: the core of Abigail's plan.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Cheever drawing the long needle out of the poppet's belly in close-up: the planted proof revealed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the hearth sequence: the found doll yields the 'evidence'.
storyboard.addedInformation: The needle turns a harmless doll into proof of witchcraft.

storyboard.claim: The incentives now allow murder through planted evidence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only beat: the abstract conclusion of the needle scene stated plainly after three photographs.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the mechanism the poppet sequence just showed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Frames the trick as a system-level weapon, not a one-off.

image.subject: Abigail Williams, a striking young Puritan woman with long dark hair escaping a white linen cap, plain grey wool dress with a white collar and apron, intense dark eyes, Salem 1692, sitting on a crowded wooden courtroom bench and watching sideways with intense eyes as Mary Warren, the timid servant in brown, sews a small cloth rag doll and pushes a needle into it for safekeeping, in the Salem meetinghouse

storyboard.claim: Abigail sat beside Mary and saw her stick the needle into the doll.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Abigail's sidelong stare at Mary's hands pushing the needle into the doll: the moment she learns the plan's ingredient.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Flashback that explains 120; starts the Abigail sequence (watch -> stab -> evidence).
storyboard.addedInformation: Abigail knew exactly where the needle was.

image.subject: Abigail Williams, a striking young Puritan woman with long dark hair escaping a white linen cap, plain grey wool dress with a white collar and apron, intense dark eyes, Salem 1692, doubled over at a candlelit wooden supper table clutching her stomach and crying out, an overturned pewter cup and a long sewing needle on the table, a startled Puritan household rising around her

storyboard.claim: Abigail stabs herself at dinner and blames Elizabeth's spirit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Abigail clutching her stomach at the supper table, needle beside her plate, household recoiling: the staged attack.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Abigail, next step: the watched needle becomes her self-inflicted wound.
storyboard.addedInformation: Weaponizes the court: a private act staged as a supernatural assault.

left.label: SPECTRAL
left.subject: an empty wooden witness stand in a dim Puritan meetinghouse courtroom, pale light falling on nothing, Salem 1692

right.label: PHYSICAL
right.subject: a small handmade cloth rag doll lying on a court clerk's wooden table beside a quill and papers, a long steel sewing needle laid next to it, Salem 1692

storyboard.claim: Spectral evidence is unprovable; Abigail supplies physical proof, turning Mary's sewing into manufactured evidence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two halves: an empty witness stand where nothing can be shown vs the needle-pierced poppet on a clerk's table as an exhibit.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the 122-123 sequence: the needle now sits as evidence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Explains why the trick works: it ends the argument over invisible proof.

image.subject: Rebecca Nurse, a gentle white-haired Puritan grandmother in her seventies, lined kind face, grey wool dress, white shawl and white linen cap, Salem 1692, and Elizabeth Proctor, the Puritan wife in dark blue, being led in iron chains up a muddy village road toward a timber jail by constables, while Reverend John Hale, the young clergyman in black, stands at the roadside watching in dismay

storyboard.claim: Rebecca Nurse and Elizabeth are taken away, and it breaks Hale.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Hale watching the two most respected women led away in chains: the cause of his doubt in one frame.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the Hale sequence (sees -> doubts).
storyboard.addedInformation: Even the town's most respected women are no longer safe.

storyboard.claim: Hale doubts the court: if Rebecca is tainted, nothing stops the world from burning.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation: Hale's own words carry the turn.
storyboard.onScreenText: "If Rebecca is tainted, nothing's left to stop the whole green world from burning."
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Hale, his reaction to 125.
storyboard.addedInformation: The court's internal logic is collapsing even for its own expert.

image.subject: Mary Warren, a timid, mousy eighteen-year-old servant girl with light brown hair under a white cap, a plain brown wool dress and patched apron, Salem 1692, sitting close beside Abigail Williams, a striking young Puritan woman with long dark hair escaping a white linen cap, plain grey wool dress with a white collar and apron, intense dark eyes, Salem 1692, on a courtroom bench, Abigail leaning in to whisper in her ear while Mary looks down at her hands

storyboard.claim: One view: Mary Warren was a willing accomplice, knowing Abigail's power.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Abigail whispering into Mary's ear on the court bench: the alleged partnership.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the debate about Mary (127-132), returning to the bench from 122.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the accomplice reading of Mary.

storyboard.claim: Did Mary plant the needle knowingly? The hosts disagree.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only question card: the disagreement itself is the point.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pivot of the Mary debate.
storyboard.addedInformation: Marks a host disagreement.

storyboard.claim: The other host thinks Mary is given too much credit for foresight.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only banter beat.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues the disagreement.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up the pawn reading.

image.subject: Mary Warren, a timid, mousy eighteen-year-old servant girl with light brown hair under a white cap, a plain brown wool dress and patched apron, Salem 1692, trembling and tearful in a dark farmhouse kitchen as John Proctor, a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, grips her by the arm and confronts her

storyboard.claim: Mary is a terrified pawn; she tells Proctor she meant no harm.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor gripping the frightened Mary in his kitchen: the pawn pleading innocence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Counter-reading in the Mary debate.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mary as manipulated and frightened, not scheming.

image.subject: Mary Warren, a timid, mousy eighteen-year-old servant girl with light brown hair under a white cap, a plain brown wool dress and patched apron, Salem 1692, with her hand over her mouth in shock, staring at a small rag doll with a long needle in it held up by Ezekiel Cheever, a thin, officious court clerk in his forties in a dark brown coat, a black hat and a leather satchel of papers, Salem 1692, in a candlelit farmhouse kitchen

storyboard.claim: Mary's shock when the needle comes out is genuine; she is Abigail's victim.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mary's horrified face reacting to the needle in Cheever's hand: shock reads as innocence.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the 120 kitchen to judge Mary's reaction.
storyboard.addedInformation: Evidence for the victim reading.

image.subject: Abigail Williams, a striking young Puritan woman with long dark hair escaping a white linen cap, plain grey wool dress with a white collar and apron, intense dark eyes, Salem 1692, standing behind a seated, frightened Mary Warren, a timid, mousy eighteen-year-old servant girl with light brown hair under a white cap, a plain brown wool dress and patched apron, Salem 1692, with one hand resting possessively on Mary's shoulder in a dim courtroom

storyboard.claim: Either way, Abigail used Mary's weakness to bypass the spectral-evidence debate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Abigail's hand on Mary's shoulder from behind: one girl steering the other.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the Mary debate (127-132) with the verdict both hosts share.
storyboard.addedInformation: Abigail controlled the outcome regardless of Mary's intent.

image.subject: John Proctor, a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, tearing a paper warrant in half with both hands in fury in his candlelit farmhouse kitchen, while Ezekiel Cheever, a thin, officious court clerk in his forties in a dark brown coat, a black hat and a leather satchel of papers, Salem 1692, steps back startled

storyboard.claim: Proctor tears the warrant and realizes Salem is ruled by the vengeance of children.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor ripping the warrant in two before Cheever: rage against the order.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back to the Proctor kitchen of 118-120: the warrant's arrival ends in it being destroyed.
storyboard.addedInformation: Proctor turns from bystander to open defiance.

storyboard.claim: This leads to the peak of the systemic failure: the courtroom.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only transition card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridge from the farmhouse to the court sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Signals the climax setting.

image.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, looming from a high judge's bench in a hot crowded timber meetinghouse, as John Proctor, the bearded farmer in a leather vest, pulls the reluctant Mary Warren, the timid servant in brown, by the hand toward the witness stand

storyboard.claim: In a sweltering court, Proctor drags Mary before Danforth to tell the truth.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor pulling Mary toward the stand under Danforth's high bench: the truth brought up against power.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the courtroom sequence (kept stage 135-140).
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the judge and the stakes of Mary's testimony.

image.subject: the Salem girls, a group of four Puritan teenage girls in grey and brown wool dresses with white caps and aprons, wide frightened eyes, Salem 1692, standing in a courtroom staring and pointing up at the empty roof rafters in terror, while Mary Warren, a timid, mousy eighteen-year-old servant girl with light brown hair under a white cap, a plain brown wool dress and patched apron, Salem 1692, at the witness stand turns to look at them in confusion

storyboard.claim: As Mary testifies, the girls scream at an invisible yellow bird they claim is her spirit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The girls pointing at empty rafters while Mary turns: a performed vision drowning out testimony.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same courtroom, next step: testimony met by spectacle.
storyboard.addedInformation: The accusers turn on Mary herself.

storyboard.claim: When a system is invested in a lie, truth stops being evidence.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only principle card drawn from the courtroom scene.
storyboard.onScreenText: INVESTED IN A LIE, TRUTH IS NOT EVIDENCE
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Generalizes the yellow-bird scene.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the timeless mechanism.

image.subject: Mary Warren, a timid, mousy eighteen-year-old servant girl with light brown hair under a white cap, a plain brown wool dress and patched apron, Salem 1692, collapsing to her knees in tears at a wooden witness stand while stern black-robed magistrates on the high bench look down on her in a crowded Puritan courtroom

storyboard.claim: Truth is treated as a threat, so Mary's testimony collapses to protect the court's authority.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Mary breaking down on her knees under the magistrates' bench: the truth-teller crushed.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of 136 in the same courtroom.
storyboard.addedInformation: Mary's testimony fails.

image.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, at his high bench with his hand resting on a thick stack of signed death warrants, staring coldly down at the witness stand in the Salem meetinghouse

storyboard.claim: Danforth wants to disbelieve Mary because believing her means admitting he hanged innocents.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Danforth's hand on the pile of signed death warrants: the past he must defend.
storyboard.onScreenText: BELIEVING HER = ADMITTING HE HANGED INNOCENTS
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same court; explains why 138 happened.
storyboard.addedInformation: Danforth's personal stake in the lie.

image.subject: Abigail Williams, a striking young Puritan woman with long dark hair escaping a white linen cap, plain grey wool dress with a white collar and apron, intense dark eyes, Salem 1692, standing in the courtroom with arms raised toward the rafters and eyes wide, performing terror, while Deputy Governor Danforth, the periwigged judge, leans forward from the bench watching her intently

storyboard.claim: Abigail hands Danforth the theatrical justification he needs.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Abigail performing at the rafters with Danforth leaning in: a show that a judge accepts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the courtroom sequence; leads to Proctor's move.
storyboard.addedInformation: Danforth gets his pretext.

image.subject: John Proctor, a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, standing before the judges' bench in a packed courtroom with his fist pressed to his chest, head bowed in shame, as the crowd recoils

storyboard.claim: The legal route failed, so Proctor sacrifices his reputation and confesses adultery.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor's fist to his chest, head bowed before the bench, crowd recoiling: public self-accusation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the confession sequence (141-145) in the same courtroom.
storyboard.addedInformation: Proctor gives up his good name as his last weapon.

image.subject: Elizabeth Proctor, a composed Puritan wife in her thirties, brown hair hidden under a white linen coif, dark blue wool dress with a plain white collar and apron, restrained grave expression, Salem 1692, being led by a constable through a side door into a crowded courtroom toward the judge's bench

storyboard.claim: He brands himself a lecher to prove Abigail's motive, and Danforth brings Elizabeth in to verify.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth led into the court as the witness who will decide it.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Next step: the confession must be tested.
storyboard.addedInformation: Brings the one witness who can confirm it.

image.subject: John Proctor, a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, and Abigail Williams, the dark-haired young woman in grey, standing with their backs to the room facing a timber courtroom wall, while Deputy Governor Danforth, the periwigged judge, questions a grave woman in a white coif at the bench

storyboard.claim: Danforth makes them turn their backs and asks Elizabeth if John is a lecher.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor and Abigail facing the wall while Danforth questions Elizabeth: the staged test.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same courtroom; the test is set up.
storyboard.addedInformation: No signal can pass between husband and wife.

image.subject: Elizabeth Proctor, a composed Puritan wife in her thirties, brown hair hidden under a white linen coif, dark blue wool dress with a plain white collar and apron, restrained grave expression, Salem 1692, standing in a courtroom gazing in anguish at the turned back of her husband, a broad-shouldered farmer in a rough brown linen shirt facing the wall

storyboard.claim: Elizabeth, who never lies, looks at her husband's back.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Elizabeth staring at John's turned back: the moment of choice.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Continues 143 from Elizabeth's side.
storyboard.addedInformation: The weight of her decision.

storyboard.claim: She tells her only lie, 'No, sir,' and it damns them both.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only punchline: the two words decide the tragedy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the confession sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Her loyalty destroys his defense.

image.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, seated at the high bench with his fingers steepled, calmly watching a broken bearded farmer weep before him in the Salem courtroom

storyboard.claim: One view: Danforth is a cold politician who knows Proctor's agonized confession is true.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Danforth's calm steepled fingers above a weeping man: knowledge without mercy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Danforth debate (146-151).
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the cynical reading.

image.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, signing a death warrant with a quill pen at a candlelit table, a coiled noose rope hanging on the wall behind him

storyboard.claim: He will hang innocents to keep the illusion of infallible justice.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Danforth signing a death warrant under a hanging rope: power protected by executions.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Danforth, cynical reading continued.
storyboard.addedInformation: His incentive is the state's authority.

image.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, kneeling in fervent prayer with eyes closed and hands clasped over an open Bible in a bare candlelit chamber

storyboard.claim: Counter-view: Danforth is a blind fanatic who believes he does God's work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Danforth praying over the Bible: sincere belief rather than calculation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Danforth, opposite reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the fanatic reading.

left.label: FANATIC
left.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, praying over an open Bible by candlelight

right.label: CYNIC
right.subject: Deputy Governor Danforth, a stern grey-haired colonial judge in his sixties in a black judicial robe with white bands and a long powdered periwig, cold heavy-lidded eyes, Massachusetts 1692, signing a stack of death warrants with a quill pen

storyboard.claim: He believes the girls because it fits his binary theology; fanaticism and cynicism wear the same face.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two halves: Danforth praying over a Bible vs Danforth signing warrants — the same man.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Combines 147 and 148.
storyboard.addedInformation: The two readings converge.

storyboard.claim: Danforth: a person is either with this court or counted against it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only quotation: the ultimatum itself.
storyboard.onScreenText: "A person is either with this court or he must be counted against it."
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Evidence for the dictator reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: His binary ultimatum.

image.subject: Elizabeth Proctor, a composed Puritan wife in her thirties, brown hair hidden under a white linen coif, dark blue wool dress with a plain white collar and apron, restrained grave expression, Salem 1692, being led away in iron chains by a constable as John Proctor, the bearded farmer in a leather vest, is held back by two constables, reaching toward her, in a crowded courtroom

storyboard.claim: Regardless of motive, Elizabeth's lie destroyed John's defense.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Husband and wife pulled apart by constables: the consequence of the lie.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes the Danforth debate on the shared result.
storyboard.addedInformation: Both Proctors are now condemned.

storyboard.claim: The system demands a lie, but one man finds a loophole.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only transition card.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Bridge to the Giles Corey sequence.
storyboard.addedInformation: Sets up a different kind of resistance.

image.subject: a bare muddy field outside a timber jail under a grey sky, a pile of heavy fieldstones stacked beside a rough wooden plank on the ground, a weathered patched brown farm coat left lying in the grass, Salem 1692

storyboard.claim: Outside the jail, stones are laid on Giles Corey; he stays mute.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Stones and an abandoned farm coat beside the plank in an empty field: pressing shown as aftermath.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the Giles sequence (153-161) on one kept place: the field by the jail.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces Giles's silent resistance.

image.subject: Giles Corey, a wiry, weathered farmer in his eighties, white stubble beard and bald crown, patched brown farm coat and breeches, Salem 1692, standing before the judges' bench in a Puritan courtroom with his lips pressed shut and arms folded, refusing to answer a clerk reading an indictment

storyboard.claim: He refuses to say aye or nay to the indictment.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Giles with lips shut and arms folded before the indictment: silence as an act.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Giles, the legal refusal behind 153.
storyboard.addedInformation: The tactic: refuse to plead.

storyboard.claim: The only way to win a rigged game is to refuse to play; standing mute, he can't be condemned.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Text-only principle card.
storyboard.onScreenText: TO WIN A RIGGED GAME, REFUSE TO PLAY
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Explains 154.
storyboard.addedInformation: The legal logic of silence.

image.subject: Giles Corey, a wiry, weathered farmer in his eighties, white stubble beard and bald crown, patched brown farm coat and breeches, Salem 1692, sitting at a rough wooden table with his weathered hand flat on an old land deed, looking out a farmhouse window at his own plowed fields

storyboard.claim: Having been in court 33 times, he knew dying unconvicted kept his property from auction.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Giles's hand on the land deed facing his fields: the property he is protecting.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Giles; the motive behind the silence.
storyboard.addedInformation: His legal knowledge and goal.

image.subject: two grown farmer sons in their forties in plain brown Puritan coats standing in a plowed field behind a farmhouse, holding an old land deed between them, Salem 1692

storyboard.claim: The land passes to his sons; one host objects that calling it pure economics strips out the courage.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The sons holding the deed on the inherited field: the property saved.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of 156's calculation.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who benefits; also opens a disagreement.

image.subject: Giles Corey, a wiry, weathered farmer in his eighties, white stubble beard and bald crown, patched brown farm coat and breeches, Salem 1692, standing outside a small timber jail with his weathered hand pressed against its barred window, head bowed in guilt

storyboard.claim: Giles died from pride and guilt for casting suspicion on his wife Martha.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Giles at the jail window where his wife is held, head bowed: guilt made physical.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Giles, emotional reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: His wife was jailed because of his words.

image.subject: Giles Corey, a wiry, weathered farmer in his eighties, white stubble beard and bald crown, patched brown farm coat and breeches, Salem 1692, standing upright in a grey field outside a timber jail with his chin raised and arms folded, facing a group of black-robed magistrates

storyboard.claim: His silence was defiance against a tyrannical court.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Giles standing tall facing the magistrates: an old man refusing to bend.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same Giles, defiance reading.
storyboard.addedInformation: Moral courage behind the strategy.

left.label: THE COST
left.subject: a pile of heavy grey fieldstones beside an empty wooden plank in a bare field outside a timber jail at dusk, Salem 1692

right.label: WHAT HE KEPT
right.subject: an old land deed with a wax seal lying on a rough wooden farm table in front of a window opening onto plowed fields, Salem 1692

storyboard.claim: He weighed physical agony against his children's inheritance and kept his property and integrity.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Two halves: heavy stones in the empty field vs the land deed on the farm table — the cost and what it bought.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Result of the Giles sequence: the trade made explicit.
storyboard.addedInformation: The calculated price.

image.subject: a lone noose rope hanging from the beam of a wooden gallows on a bare hilltop against a cold grey dawn sky, an empty oxcart standing on the hill road below, Salem 1692

storyboard.claim: The final price of a name, and the last agonizing morning arrives.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Empty noose and oxcart at dawn on the hill: the execution morning shown as place.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Closes Giles and opens the ending at the gallows.
storyboard.addedInformation: Signals executions are coming.

image.subject: John Proctor, a broad-shouldered Puritan farmer in his thirties, dark unruly hair and short beard, rough brown linen shirt with rolled sleeves and a leather work vest, Salem 1692, gaunt and hollow-eyed with chains on his wrists, sitting at a rough table in a cold stone jail cell at dawn, holding a quill pen over a signed paper confession

storyboard.claim: At dawn in the jail, a hollowed Proctor has just signed a confession.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Proctor in chains with the quill above the signed paper: the act of signing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Starts the final sequence at the jail table (continues into 163-164).
storyboard.addedInformation: He has chosen to sign the lie.
